title: Catch Me If You Can
author: Andrew Marcinek
summary: Andrew Marcinek argues that AI-detection tools are the wrong response to AI-assisted writing, in schools and in publishing alike, because they can't actually measure what matters: whether a mind directed the thinking. He opens with his own test of Substack's new AI detector, which flagged his 95%-human-written post as AI while scoring a barely-edited AI draft as 30% human, and backs the anecdote with research showing no evaluated detector reaches 80% accuracy and that detectors misclassify non-native English writers as AI-generated at a 61% false-positive rate. He draws an analogy to academic research assistance, arguing that using AI the way a tenured professor uses graduate students, for legwork, not authorship, has always been considered legitimate scholarship, and that detection culture treats a century-old practice as a new form of cheating. The piece is most pointed about classrooms: since a single follow-up prompt can drop detection rates from 100% to 13%, teaching detection teaches evasion, not integrity. Citing a Harvard RCT where deliberately scaffolded AI tutoring roughly doubled learning against an MIT study where unscaffolded ChatGPT use produced the weakest brain connectivity of any group, Marcinek concludes that the instructional design of the AI interaction, not the tool's mere presence, determines whether students learn. His proposed alternative to scanning finished text is asking for the student's prompt history and revision trail, which locates the graded work in the thinking rather than in the surface of the prose.
points: Marcinek's own test of Substack's AI detector produced both a false positive (his 95%-human post flagged as AI) and a false negative (a barely-edited AI draft scored 30% human), demonstrating the tools' unreliability from direct experience.
Independent research backs up the anecdote: no evaluated detector reached 80% accuracy, and a Stanford study found a 61% false-positive rate for non-native English writers specifically.

A single follow-up prompt asking a model to 'elevate its language' dropped detection rates from 100% to 13% in Stanford's testing, meaning detection strategies teach students evasion rather than integrity.

Contrasting a Harvard RCT (scaffolded AI tutoring roughly doubled learning) against an MIT EEG study (unscaffolded ChatGPT use produced the weakest brain connectivity), Marcinek argues the design of the AI interaction determines whether learning happens.

His proposed replacement for detection is process transparency: students submit their prompt history and show what they rejected and revised, mirroring how academia has always distributed intellectual labor.
quotes: Last week I ran one of my own posts through Substack's new AI scanner. I wrote roughly 95% of it with a few assisted polishings here and there. The Substack AI Detector flagged it anyway. So I tried the reverse. I gave an AI a single prompt, took what it handed back, barely touched it, and scanned that. 30% human.

The most comprehensive independent test of AI-text detectors, published in the International Journal for Educational Integrity, found that none of the fourteen tools evaluated reached 80 percent accuracy, and performance fell apart further once text was edited or paraphrased.

A Stanford study in Patterns found detectors misclassified essays by non-native English writers as AI-generated at an average false positive rate of 61 percent, while handling native-speaker essays nearly perfectly. What these tools actually flag is a style, and they punish writers whose style doesn't fit the pattern.
That same Stanford team found that a single follow-up prompt asking the model to elevate its language dropped detection rates from 100 percent to 13. Students will learn that trick in a week.

A randomized controlled trial at Harvard found students learned more than twice as much in less time with an AI tutor, but that tutor was built deliberately around pedagogical best practice, giving one step at a time and refusing to hand over full solutions. The design did the work, not the model.
So the assignment can't be "don't use AI," and it can't be "we'll catch you if you do." The assignment is: bring me your prompt history. Show me what the first draft gave you and what you rejected.
